title: Deals, Lesson 6: The fairness opinion and the duties of the board
subtitle: Who protects minority shareholders, what the investment bank is actually signing, and why the conflict of interest is structural
whyItMatters: The seller's board decides on behalf of thousands of shareholders who have no voice in the negotiation. A fairness opinion is the formal instrument used to show they discharged that duty properly - and understanding the limits of the instrument matters just as much as understanding the instrument itself.
openingQuestion: What does a fairness opinion issued by an investment bank assert?
openingOptions: That this is the best price obtainable anywhere in the market
That the price merely falls within a reasonable range financially
That the deal will benefit both parties to it
That the target business has been fully diligenced
explanation: This is a document routinely read as saying more than it does. It does not say best price, it does not say the deal should be done, and it does not substitute for due diligence. It asserts one narrow thing: that from a financial point of view, this price falls within a reasonable range for shareholders as at the date of issue, based on the valuation methods and assumptions set out in the document itself. Its legal value lies in showing that the board took independent advice before deciding.

diagram.label: The board decides on behalf of shareholders
It engages an adviser to issue an independent opinion
The opinion: is the price within a reasonable range
Shareholders vote on the basis of that file

realWorldExample.company: The conflict of interest in how advisory fees are paid
realWorldExample.description: An investment bank advising the seller is usually paid a success fee - payable only if the deal completes, and proportional to deal value. If that same bank also issues the fairness opinion, it is being paid for the deal to happen and simultaneously asked to judge objectively whether the price is fair. Good practice is to engage a different firm to issue the opinion on a fixed fee that does not depend on the outcome. In shareholder litigation, the fee arrangement is one of the first things put under question.

quiz.question: What is the primary duty of the seller's board in a deal?
options: To preserve every employee's job at the business for at least three years afterwards
To ensure the deal completes on the timetable committed to the buyer in the term sheet
To act in the best interests of shareholders, even where that conflicts with their own interests
To choose the bidder with the strongest financial resources among all the valid offers received
quiz.explanation: The second half is the important part: management may lose their jobs, or conversely benefit enormously from the deal, and this duty exists precisely because of those conflicts. Job preservation may be negotiated but is not the legal duty, sticking to a timetable serves the buyer rather than the shareholders, and the strongest balance sheet is only one input into deal certainty rather than the objective itself.

quiz.question: Why is the fairness opinion usually commissioned from a different firm than the deal adviser?
options: Because engaging two separate firms usually costs less than giving the whole mandate to a single firm
Because a single firm is barred by the regulator from both advising and issuing the opinion
Because the firm issuing the opinion needs a separate licence that investment banks do not hold
Because the deal adviser earns a success fee, so it has a financial interest in the deal completing
quiz.explanation: This is a structural conflict rather than a matter of individual ethics, so the remedy has to be structural too: split the roles and pay a fixed fee. Two firms cost more rather than less, no rule bars one firm from doing both in most jurisdictions, and issuing a fairness opinion requires no special licence beyond the advisory permissions the bank already has.

quiz.question: What does a no-shop clause in the agreement do?
options: It stops the seller actively looking for another buyer after signing with the current one
It stops the buyer approaching the seller's key personnel before the deal formally completes
It stops both sides disclosing information about the deal externally before announcement day
It stops the seller's shareholders transferring shares between signing and closing
quiz.explanation: The clause normally comes with a carve-out allowing the board to consider a superior proposal if another party approaches unsolicited - precisely because a duty owed to shareholders cannot be contracted away entirely. Non-solicitation of employees, confidentiality and transfer restrictions are all separate clauses that address different risks in the same agreement.

quiz.question: What is the most important limitation of a fairness opinion?
options: It remains valid for only thirty days from the date on which the advisory firm formally issues it to the board
It assesses the price at one point in time and does not assert this is the best available option
It cannot be used as evidence in any legal dispute arising after the deal has completed
It applies only to deals whose value exceeds a certain threshold under the rules in force
quiz.explanation: A price can be simultaneously within a reasonable range and lower than what a more competitive sale process would have achieved. The opinion does not answer that second question at all. There is no thirty-day statutory life, the document is routinely used as evidence in litigation, and no value threshold governs when one may be obtained.

quiz.question: Does holding a fairness opinion exempt the board from liability when shareholders sue?
options: Yes, because liability transfers to the firm that issued the opinion
Yes, provided the opinion was issued before the board formally voted
No, it is evidence of a careful process rather than a shield
No, because shareholders cannot sue over a board decision at all
quiz.explanation: The board's duty of care remains the board's - a single document cannot buy it out. What gets examined is the whole process: was another party invited to bid, was the adviser's conflict of interest handled, were alternatives to this deal considered. The fairness opinion is one link in that chain. Liability does not transfer to the issuer, timing alone confers no protection, and shareholders can and regularly do sue.

keyTakeaways: A fairness opinion only says the price sits within a reasonable range at one point in time, not that it is the best price
The board owes a duty to shareholders even when it runs against their own interests
A success fee creates a structural conflict: separate the opinion role and pay a fixed fee
A no-shop clause usually comes with a carve-out for a superior proposal arriving from outside
A fair price and the best price are two different questions - this document answers only the first

practicePrompt.question: The board accepts the first offer it receives, supported by a fairness opinion. Shareholders sue, arguing there was no competitive process. Does that opinion protect the board?
options: Yes, because an independent firm confirmed the price was fair
Not really: it proves the price was reasonable, not the best
No, because the opinion carries no legal weight at all
Yes, if it was issued by a firm taking no success fee
practicePrompt.explanation: This is the boundary most often confused in the whole lesson. A fairness opinion speaks to the outcome - the price. The shareholders' complaint here speaks to the process - whether the board did enough to find a better price. The two are assessed separately, and a supportive opinion does not automatically answer the question about process.

summary.keyIdea: A fairness opinion assesses the price, not the quality of the process that arrived at that price
summary.commonMistake: Treating the opinion as a statement that the deal is the best available option for shareholders
summary.action: Find the fairness opinion section in a shareholder proxy document and read the limitations paragraph closely.

application.title: What to do
application.message: Open the proxy document for a deal that has been announced. Find the section describing the fairness opinion and answer three questions: which firm issued it, how were they paid, and what limitations does the document itself set out on its conclusion.
application.secondary: The limitations section is usually longer than the conclusion, and it tells you exactly what the document is not asserting.

sections.text: This stage closes on the least technical question of all, and the one with the most real consequences: who is responsible when a deal is agreed, and what do they rely on when they sign.
Two different questions, and one document that answers only one

left.label: The question about price
left.text: Does this price fall within a reasonable range from a financial point of view. That is the question a fairness opinion answers, using the valuation methods covered in the valuation section.

right.label: The question about process
right.text: Did the board do enough to find the best available option: was there a competitive sale, was the conflict of interest handled, were other offers considered. The other document does not answer this.

sections.title: The mechanisms that protect minority shareholders
sections.subtitle: No mechanism is sufficient alone; they compensate for one another

concepts.def: Confirms the price sits within a reasonable range. Strongest when issued by a firm that takes no success fee.
Made up of directors with no interest in the deal, negotiating on behalf of the whole board. Most important when management is also the buyer.
A large deal has to be approved by the shareholders' meeting. This is the last line of defence and the reason the file sent to shareholders has to be complete.

sections.label: When management stands on both sides
sections.text: The hardest case is when management itself takes part in buying the company it runs. They know the true value better than anyone and have a direct interest in buying cheaply. Here a fairness opinion is not enough: practice requires an independent committee with the authority to engage its own adviser and to refuse the deal, together with the exclusion of the interested parties from voting.

lines: A document confirming that a price is reasonable does not replace a process that goes looking for a better one.
This stage closes the deal mechanics: from the first EPS calculation to the final signature.
